disputes: Concept and truth: the IEP says the concept 'has no relationship to truth, which is an external determination'; What Is Philosophy? says a concept always has 'the truth that falls to it', according to the conditions of its creation (p. 27) and that philosophy is not inspired by truth (p. 82). Both are stated in Plane of immanence; how far they differ is left open.

Conceptual personae and subjects: the Stanford article says a conceptual persona is not a subject, since thinking is not subjective; the book calls the personae 'the real subjects of his philosophy' and 'the becoming or the subject of a philosophy' (p. 64), while also saying the one who says 'I' is always a third person (p. 65). The article's sense of 'subject' may be the psychological one the book also rejects; both are quoted, each credited.

One plane per philosopher: the IEP and the previous entry said each philosopher must create a plane; the book asks whether each great philosopher does (p. 51) and records philosophers working on a master's plane (p. 57). The book leans toward it (p. 51) and qualifies it (p. 57); the entry states both pages.

Difference and Repetition: the IEP links the plane of immanence to that book's image of thought; the text of What Is Philosophy? does not name it (searched; the scan's notes are damaged, and the back cover's author note does name it). Recorded as the IEP's reading.

new_d.text: In What Is Philosophy? (1991), the plane a philosophy lays out as the presupposition of its concepts: the image thought gives itself of what it means to think, which Deleuze and Guattari call the absolute ground of philosophy.

new_text.text: What Is Philosophy?, published in 1991, a year before Guattari's death (translators' introduction, p. vii), calls philosophy “the art of forming, inventing, and fabricating concepts” (p. 2), then says it is not simply such an art, since concepts are not necessarily forms, discoveries or products; its object is to create concepts that are always new (p. 5).
Science creates functions on a plane of reference (p. 118), and art creates blocs of sensation, compounds of percepts and affects (p. 164).

“Thought, in all its modes,” the Stanford Encyclopedia article adds, “struggles with chaos against opinion”; the book's conclusion calls the struggle with chaos the instrument of a deeper struggle against opinion (p. 206).
Pages of What Is Philosophy? are from the translation by Hugh Tomlinson and Graham Burchell (1994).
Every concept, the first chapter holds, has components and is defined by them: it is a multiplicity, and there are no simple concepts (p. 15).
Its components are “distinct, heterogeneous, and yet not separable”, and their inseparability defines the concept's consistency (pp. 19–20).

The concept is not a proposition (p. 22), and it always has “the truth that falls to it”, according to the conditions of its creation (p. 27); the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy says it “has no relationship to truth, which is an external determination”.
Concepts are created on a plane, which the second chapter calls a plane of consistency or, more accurately, “the plane of immanence of concepts, the planomenon” (p. 35).
Concepts and plane are strictly correlative, and yet the plane is neither a concept nor the concept of all concepts (p. 35).

It is “the image thought gives itself of what it means to think” (p. 37); it is prephilosophical, presupposed by philosophy and instituted by it (pp. 40–41); and it acts like a sieve, a section of chaos (p. 42).
The authors ask whether every great philosopher lays out a new plane, and cannot imagine a great philosopher who has not changed what it means to think (p. 51).

Those who do not renew the image of thought they deny the name of philosopher and call functionaries (p. 51); yet philosophers can create new concepts for a long time on the plane of an earlier philosopher they take as their master, as the neo-Platonists did with Plato, extending that plane until it is doubtful whether it is still the same one (p. 57).
The question of what thought presupposes, the IEP notes, is the one Difference and Repetition had treated under the image of thought; the text of What Is Philosophy? does not name that book.
Conceptual personae carry out the movements of a philosopher's plane and take part in creating the concepts (p. 63).
Descartes's is the Idiot, the private thinker who says “I” and lays out the plane (pp. 61–62).

The philosopher, the authors write, is only the envelope of his conceptual personae, “the real subjects of his philosophy” (p. 64); the Stanford article writes that “a conceptual persona is not a subject, for thinking is not subjective.”

Immanence, the authors write, “is immanent only to itself”; whenever it is interpreted as immanent to something, that something reintroduces the transcendent (p. 45), and transcendence enters as soon as the movement of the infinite is stopped (p. 47).

Spinoza, who knew that immanence was immanent only to itself, is “the prince of philosophers” (p. 48) and “the Christ of philosophers”, who drew up the purest plane (p. 60); Deleuze's essay “Immanence: A Life” returns to the theme.
A Thousand Plateaus already speaks of a plane of immanence.

Its tenth plateau, in the sections it calls “Memories of a Spinozist”, describes a fixed plane on which things are distinguished only by speed and slowness, “a plane of immanence or univocality opposed to analogy” (pp. 253–254).

The authors call it the plane of consistency or composition, as opposed to the plan(e) of organization or development, and “necessarily a plane of immanence and univocality”; on it there is no distinction between the natural and the artificial, and it never has a dimension supplementary to what happens on it (p. 266).
The plane of organization and development they call the plane of transcendence (p. 281).
Pages of A Thousand Plateaus are from Brian Massumi's translation (1987).

Philosophy, the authors write, keeps the infinite and gives the virtual consistency through concepts; science gives up the infinite and gives the virtual a reference that actualizes it through functions (p. 118).
The Stanford article reads this as philosophy mapping the forces of a system as pure potentials, while science explains why one road was taken.

deterritorialization.new: What Is Philosophy? carries the terms into philosophy itself: deterritorialization is relative when it concerns the earth's historical relationship with territories, its geological relationship with eras and catastrophes, or its astronomical relationship with the cosmos, and absolute “when the earth passes into the pure plane of immanence of a Being-thought” (p. 88); philosophy, the authors write, is reterritorialized on the concept (p. 101).

deterritorialization.new: The Stanford article classes deterritorialization among philosophy's concepts, which the authors keep apart in kind from the functions of science (pp. 117–118), and notes that they repeatedly insist such concepts are no metaphors.
deterritorialization.note: The concept/function distinction is in the book (pp. 117–118). The word 'metaphor' does not occur in What Is Philosophy? (searched in the scan's text layer); the 'no metaphors' claim rests on the article.

summary: Plane of immanence read in What Is Philosophy?: page numbers throughout and Deleuze and Guattari credited for what the book says (Spinoza as 'the prince' and 'the Christ of philosophers', the Idiot, immanence immanent only to itself). The claim that every philosopher must lay out a plane of their own is restated as the book has it, a question it leans toward (p. 51) and qualifies (p. 57); the book's 'real subjects' is set beside the Stanford article's 'not a subject', and its 'truth that falls to' a concept beside the IEP's 'no relationship to truth'. Deterritorialization gains the book's relative and absolute deterritorialization (p. 88).
